extracted.intended_audience: stage magicians and touring performing artists; theatre managers and impresarios
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, performance-and-production guidance for staging, programming, and managing touring stage magic shows (audience selection, visibility, logistics, publicity) drawn from a performer's memoir. Emphasis on adapting tricks, language, and stagecraft to venue and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose effects suited to venue size and audience distance
rubrics_metrics.description: “je fus obligé de composer un programme, dans lequel il n'y aurait que des prestiges qui pussent être vus de loin, et dont l'effet frappât les masses.” (I was obliged to compose a programme containing only prestiges that could be seen from afar and whose effect struck the masses.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select tricks and illusions whose visual scale and impact match the size of the theatre; in very large houses prefer big, broadly visible effects rather than delicate close-up pieces. Example/anti-pattern: intimate sleight-of-hand that thrills a small parterre will be lost in a Roman-sized hall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt language and interact to bridge language barriers
rubrics_metrics.description: When confronted with demands like “speack english,” the performer tried some words of English and used invented expressions, audience questions and comedic seriousness (e.g., 'How do you call it?') to engage the crowd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you cannot fluently speak the audience's language, use simple phrases, comic seriousness, invented turns of phrase and direct audience participation to keep engagement and turn the language barrier into a feature rather than a flaw.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control stage access; refuse outsiders onto the stage
rubrics_metrics.description: The performer insists no stranger may penetrate his stage — e.g., he refused the Baron Brunow's attempt to enter and said 'aucun étranger ne doit pénétrer sur ma scène.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain strict control of who goes onto the stage to protect secrets, safety and artistic order. Politely but firmly refuse unsolicited people (even dignitaries) unless you explicitly invite them; provide a controlled mechanism for VIP guests if required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use prominent endorsements and publicity to increase reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: After performing for the Queen, posters were printed with royal arms and the legend 'Robert-Houdin who has had the honor to perform before her most gracious Majesty...' which increased vogue at Saint-James.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secure permission to cite notable patrons and include such endorsements prominently in advertising and posters to boost audience draw and prestige.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate crowd behavior when offering physical giveaways (safety and logistics)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'inexhaustible bottle' routine, when distributing drinks among hundreds, produced pushing, fighting, broken glass and a human pyramid that almost overwhelmed the performer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan distribution mechanics carefully; limit simultaneous access, use controlled serving methods (aisles, ushers, staged distribution) to avoid fights, breakage, injuries and loss of control. Consider safety and crowding before adding audience-consumable elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design stage layout for visibility and audience access
rubrics_metrics.description: A practicable floor extended from stage to the parterre and two shorter side practicables were placed to address side galleries; side practicables were located above passages so they did not occupy seats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible create extensions/protruding platforms so performers can reach front and side audiences. Arrange practicables to maximize sightlines without occupying seats; consider passages and how latecomers will move.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match repertoire and tone to audience demographics
rubrics_metrics.description: At Saint-James the fashionable, aristocratic audience preferred refined effects; at Manchester the working-class crowd wanted large-gestured, mass-visible prestiges and lively, brash demonstrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt content, pacing and tone to the socio-economic composition of the audience: mass workers favor bold, participatory and boisterous effects; elite audiences appreciate subtlety and refinement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve a big finale (a strong concluding effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: The performer structured shows so the last experiment (the bottle culminating in an enormous glass) would serve as the coup de fouet — the final flourish of the evening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan show arcs to build toward a memorable, high-impact finale that secures audience acclaim and recalls; saving a spectacular effect for the end increases the chance of encores and positive reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid exhausting local curiosity through overexposure
rubrics_metrics.description: A cautionary lesson: 'il est dangereux... d'épuiser trop à fond la curiosité publique' — after too many shows in a locality audience size can sharply decline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit consecutive performances in the same town to preserve demand; monitor attendance and decline early rather than overstay and damage future draws. Consider spacing returns to a locality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage press reviews and critics to affect attendance
rubrics_metrics.description: In England some people waited to read the feuilletoniste's account in the paper before deciding to attend; the review could make or break later houses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate favorable press coverage; time performances relative to expected reviews; understand local critics’ influence on turnout and reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be prepared for rapid teardown and protection of apparatus in multi-use venues
rubrics_metrics.description: At Buckingham Palace, after the show workers immediately began dismantling the theatre for a ball; the performer had to pack machines in an hour and a half to avoid breakage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have packing plans, protective cases, and trained crews ready to disassemble quickly when venues must be returned to other uses. Anticipate conflicting schedules in multi-purpose or royal venues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schedule and tour according to seasonality and local customs
rubrics_metrics.description: In England the season of concerts, fêtes and spectacles runs May through August; once September arrives the nobility return to country manors and social life quiets down.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan touring calendar around local social seasons—peak months for public entertainments vary by country and class. Time major engagements to overlap with local high season.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage audience orderliness before beginning (allow time to settle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before opening, the performer waited to let his 'bruyant public' calm down; order and silence were restored before he began.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not start until the audience has settled; build a brief period to restore order if necessary, using stage business or opening patter to channel energy productively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Train and use reliable assistants (including family) effectively on stage
rubrics_metrics.description: The performer's children and secretary assisted with preparations and onstage tasks (e.g., son performed 'second sight' and fetched glasses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop trusted assistants who know the show’s timing and emergency improvisations. Use them for delicate tasks, audience control and improvisational cover when things go awry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider dynamic pricing and workforce adjustments when demand spikes
rubrics_metrics.description: The regisseur advised doubling prices and increasing staff when large demand was expected in a town.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When demand justifies it, adjust pricing and personnel levels to maximize revenue and maintain order. Balance higher prices against public perception and long-term goodwill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect secrets from curious, perceptive observers
rubrics_metrics.description: He cited refusing Baron Brunow and noting the baron's 'perspicacité' — performers should avoid giving away confidences to those likely to deduce methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guard methods and backstage procedures from keen or presumptuous individuals; use discretion in what is revealed and enforce backstage access restrictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Turn mishaps into comic or engaging moments (improvisation)
rubrics_metrics.description: When his English vocabulary failed, the performer invented phrases and solicited audience help, making the 'lesson' amusing and paid for by spectators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When something goes wrong, improvise confidently and use it to create a fresh, participatory moment. Skilled improvisation can win audience sympathy and convert error into entertainment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt set and costume aesthetics to the venue/context
rubrics_metrics.description: At Buckingham the stage represented a Louis XV salon similar to Saint-James; presentation matched the royal setting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Style scenic design and costume to suit the tastes and expectations of the host venue and its patrons to increase perceived appropriateness and impact.
